Glass fibre composites were the first to be used for aircraft structures, with the Vultee BT-15 trainer aircraft being made and flown in 1944.
Graphite fibres were first developed in the UK, while boron fibres were developed in the USA.
The US had made and flown major boron/epoxy demonstrator items by 1970.
The cost of graphite/epoxy material in the USA was $40 per lb. in 1979.
The Boeing 737 spoilers were made of graphite/epoxy and achieved 22,000 flight hours without significant problems.
The NASA ACEE program aims to provide technology and confidence for commercial transport manufacturers to use composites in their future aircraft.
The Boeing 757 and 767 aircraft use graphite/epoxy for many of their control surfaces.
The Lear Fan 2100 aircraft is an 'all-composite' aircraft with almost all its airframe made of composites.
Graphite/epoxy is used in the Space Shuttle's cargo bay doors.
Aramid/epoxy is widely used in aircraft structures, but its low compressive strength limits its use in primary structure.
The Boeing 767 uses a hybrid aramid-graphite composite for its wing-to-fuselage fairing and other components.
The F-14 aircraft uses boron/epoxy for its horizontal tail skin.
The F-15 aircraft uses boron/epoxy for its horizontal and vertical tail skins.
The F-16 aircraft uses graphite/epoxy for its horizontal and vertical tail skins and control surfaces.
